drafts.title: $0.39 per kWh and no app: Plug & Charge comes to IONNA and Electrify America
drafts.angle: The best charger upgrade this year is boring. You plug in and it just bills you, like a Supercharger. That matters most for drivers who hate phone apps.
bullets: IONNA turned on Plug & Charge for Tesla drivers, with Stellantis 'coming soon' (Electrek, Nov 18).
IONNA's new 22-bay, 400 kW Westminster CA site: promo $0.20/kWh for the first weeks, then standard $0.39/kWh.
GM enabled Plug & Charge at Electrify America for Blazer EV, Equinox EV, Sierra EV, Lyriq and Optiq (GM Energy Pass members).
The pain it fixes: fumbling with apps, card readers and bad cell signal at a cold charger.
drafts.body: $0.39 per kWh and no app to fight with. IONNA now lets Teslas just plug in and charge. GM drivers got the same thing at Electrify America. My worst charger moment: {my app or card reader story}. What's the most annoying part of public charging for you?
drafts.framework_body:
$0.39 per kWh, and no app to fight with.

That's the news I've been waiting on. IONNA just turned on Plug & Charge for Teslas. You plug in, the car and charger talk to each other, and it bills you. No app, no card reader, no hunting for cell signal in a cold parking lot.

GM drivers got the same thing this week at Electrify America. Blazer, Equinox, Sierra, Lyriq and Optiq owners can plug in and walk away.

My worst charger moment: {my app or card reader story}.

At home I pay about {what I pay per kWh at home}, so public charging is never my cheapest option. But on the road, the price is only half of it. The other half is whether the thing just works.

This matters most for older drivers. A lot of folks I talk to aren't scared of EVs. They're scared of standing at a charger with five apps and none of them working.

Plug in. Walk away. That's how every charger should work.

What's the most annoying part of public charging for you?

drafts.framework_body:
$3 billion plant, one goal: a cheaper electric pickup.

Ford's battery plant in Marshall, Michigan is now shipping cells. The first ones are going into prototypes of the Fathom, Ford's small electric pickup.

These are LFP batteries. Plain English: the cheaper kind that lasts a long time and doesn't mind being charged to full every day. That's the battery you want in a work truck.

I've been shopping for a small truck for a while. My wish list is simple:
1. Priced around {price I'd pay}, not luxury money.
2. {range I need in winter} of real winter range out here in western Colorado.
3. A bed that fits {what I haul}.

I don't need 0 to 60 in three seconds. I need it to haul stuff and not cost more than a gas truck.

If Ford gets the price right, a lot of working families are going to look at an electric pickup for the first time.

Would you buy a small electric pickup if it was priced like a gas one?

drafts.title: $1.50: the fake delivery text that wants your card
drafts.topic: AI for normal people / holiday scams
drafts.angle: Everybody has a package coming this month. Scammers know it, and AI makes their texts look perfect now. Share-to-your-parents save.
bullets: US Treasury issued its annual holiday scam advisory Nov 18, warning crooks use AI to impersonate trusted people, businesses and loved ones.
Common play: a text says your parcel is stuck until you pay a tiny fee (Swiss NCSC example: CHF 1.50) or confirm your address. The link steals your card.
Barclays survey (Nov 13): 76% say AI makes scams more convincing, but only 36% check a site is real before buying, and 34% feel confident spotting an AI scam.
Fix: never tap the link. Open the carrier's app or site yourself and type in the tracking number.
drafts.body: $1.50. That's all the fake delivery text asks for. It's not about the $1.50. It's your card number. My rule: {my rule for package texts}. Have you or your parents gotten one of these yet?
drafts.framework_body:
$1.50.

That's all the fake delivery text asks for. Your package is stuck, pay a small fee or confirm your address.

It's not about the $1.50. It's your card number.

The Treasury Department just put out its holiday scam warning, and the big change this year is AI. These texts used to have bad spelling and weird grammar. Now they look exactly like the real thing.

A Barclays survey found 76% of people say AI makes scams more convincing. Only about a third feel confident they could spot one.

My rule: {my rule for package texts}.

Here's the simple version for your parents:
1. Never tap the link in a delivery text.
2. Open the UPS, FedEx, USPS or Amazon app yourself.
3. Type in the tracking number. If there's a real problem, it'll be there.

No real carrier holds your package hostage for a dollar fifty.

Have you or your parents gotten one of these yet?
drafts.ocr_why: Tiny dollar opener, everyone has a package coming, and it is a save-and-send-to-family post.
drafts.pixel: Holding phone: "If a text says your package is stuck for a dollar fifty, do this instead."
drafts.premium_target: Reply or quote a verified bank or consumer-fraud account posting holiday scam tips: "Never tap the link. Open the app yourself." Different from the Nov 16 fake stores and Nov 15 safe word posts.

drafts.title: AI explains Medicare. Medicare.gov picks the plan. Deadline Dec 7.
drafts.angle: AI is great at explaining Medicare jargon. It is not the place to pick your plan. Use both the right way before Dec 7.
bullets: Medicare open enrollment ends Dec 7, 2026.
AI chatbots can explain terms (Part D, deductible, formulary) and help write questions, but they can't reliably confirm current local plan prices, networks or drug coverage.
The real numbers: Medicare.gov Plan Finder by ZIP code, with your actual prescriptions and pharmacy.
Free human help: SHIP counselors and 1-800-MEDICARE.
drafts.body: {$XX a month} is what the wrong drug plan could cost someone I know. AI helped me understand the Medicare words. The plan check still goes on Medicare.gov with real prescriptions. Deadline is Dec 7. Has anyone in your family checked their plan this year?
drafts.framework_body:
{$XX a month}.

That's what the wrong drug plan could cost {someone I know}.

Medicare open enrollment ends December 7. And this is a place where AI really helps, if you use it right.

What AI is great at:
1. Explaining the words. Part D, formulary, deductible, out-of-pocket max. Ask it like you'd ask a patient friend.
2. Writing your questions down before you call anyone.
3. Making a simple checklist of your prescriptions and doctors.

Where AI stops:
It can't reliably tell you this year's price for a plan in your ZIP code, or whether your pharmacy and your exact drugs are covered. Plans change every year.

That part goes on Medicare.gov Plan Finder, with your real prescriptions typed in. If you want a human, SHIP counselors are free, and so is 1-800-MEDICARE.

AI explains. You verify.

Has anyone in your family checked their plan this year?
